question: A company runs a batch processing workload every night from 10 PM to 4 AM. The workload has been running consistently for 2 years and will continue for the foreseeable future. Which EC2 pricing model provides the lowest cost?

options.A: On-Demand Instances
options.B: Spot Instances
options.C: Reserved Instances (1-year, No Upfront)
options.D: Dedicated Hosts

explanation: For predictable, steady-state workloads that run consistently, Reserved Instances (RIs) provide the greatest discount (up to 72% vs On-Demand for 1-year All Upfront, or ~40% for 1-year No Upfront). The batch job runs every night reliably, making RI commitment economically justified. A 1-year Standard RI in the same AZ matches the workload duration perfectly.

distractors.A: On-Demand pricing has no commitment discount — paying full price for a predictable nightly workload is the most expensive option.
distractors.B: Spot Instances can be interrupted with a 2-minute warning — a batch job that must complete nightly cannot tolerate arbitrary interruptions without checkpoint/restart logic.
distractors.D: Dedicated Hosts provide physical server isolation for compliance purposes at a premium cost, not for cost optimization of standard workloads.

question: A company wants to commit to a consistent amount of compute usage across its entire AWS account and all instance families (not tied to a specific instance type or region). Which pricing model offers this flexibility with up to 66% savings?

options.A: Standard Reserved Instances
options.B: Convertible Reserved Instances
options.C: Compute Savings Plans
options.D: EC2 Instance Savings Plans

explanation: Compute Savings Plans offer the most flexible commitment — they apply automatically to any EC2 instance usage regardless of instance family, size, AZ, region, OS, or tenancy, and also cover AWS Fargate and Lambda. In exchange for a 1 or 3-year hourly spend commitment, you receive up to 66% savings compared to On-Demand. This is ideal for organizations with diverse or changing instance needs.

distractors.A: Standard Reserved Instances are locked to a specific instance type, AZ, and region — they provide up to 72% savings but with minimal flexibility.
distractors.B: Convertible Reserved Instances allow changing instance family/OS/tenancy within the same region but are still per-region and provide lower savings (up to 54%) than Compute Savings Plans.
distractors.D: EC2 Instance Savings Plans are locked to a specific instance family and region (but flexible within that family for size/AZ/OS), providing up to 72% savings — less flexible than Compute Savings Plans.

question: A company purchased a 1-year Standard Reserved Instance for an m5.xlarge in us-east-1a. Three months later, they migrate the application to an m6i.xlarge. What happens to the unused Standard RI?

options.A: AWS automatically converts the RI to apply to the m6i.xlarge
options.B: The RI can be modified to apply to m6i as long as the normalization factor matches
options.C: The Standard RI continues billing regardless — it can be listed on the Reserved Instance Marketplace to sell it
options.D: AWS refunds the unused portion of the Standard RI

explanation: Standard Reserved Instances are not automatically transferable to different instance families. However, unused Standard RIs can be listed on the AWS Reserved Instance Marketplace, where other AWS customers can purchase them (marketplace supports 1-year remaining minimum). Alternatively, the company pays for the RI whether or not they use it — selling on the marketplace recoups some cost.

distractors.A: Automatic conversion applies to Convertible RIs, not Standard RIs — Standard RIs are locked to the purchased instance type family.
distractors.B: Standard RI modifications allow changing instance size within the same family (e.g., m5.large to m5.xlarge) using normalization factors, but not changing the instance family from m5 to m6i.
distractors.D: AWS does not refund unused RIs — you pay for the full commitment period. Selling on the RI Marketplace is the recovery option.

question: A company has 100 On-Demand EC2 instances running 24/7. They want to optimize costs. AWS Cost Explorer shows they consistently use at least 60 instances every hour, with spikes to 100 instances. What is the optimal purchasing strategy?

options.A: Purchase 100 Reserved Instances to cover the maximum
options.B: Purchase 60 Compute Savings Plans commitments and run 40 as On-Demand for peak
options.C: Purchase 60 Compute Savings Plans commitments and run 40 as Spot Instances for peaks
options.D: Run all 100 as Spot Instances with Spot Fleet for automatic replacement

explanation: The optimal strategy layers pricing models: purchase Savings Plans (or RIs) for the consistent baseline (60 instances) at 60-72% discount, and use Spot Instances for the variable peak demand (up to 40 instances) at up to 90% discount vs On-Demand. This minimizes cost while maintaining the ability to handle spikes. On-Demand for peaks is more expensive than Spot for workloads that can tolerate interruption.

distractors.A: Purchasing 100 RIs/Savings Plans covers peak capacity but wastes money during off-peak hours when only 60 instances run — you pay for 100 commitments but use 60.
distractors.B: Using On-Demand for peak (40 instances) works but is more expensive than Spot for variable burst workloads.
distractors.D: Running all 100 as Spot saves the most money on paper but risks losing 100% of capacity if Spot prices spike — no instance is guaranteed, making this too risky for production.

question: A company wants to use Spot Instances for a fault-tolerant batch processing job. They want AWS to automatically request replacement Spot Instances if the current ones are interrupted. Which feature provides this capability?

options.A: Spot Instance with a persistent request type
options.B: EC2 Auto Scaling with Spot Instances and capacity rebalancing
options.C: Spot Fleet with maintain allocation strategy
options.D: On-Demand capacity reservation with fallback

explanation: A Spot Fleet with the `maintain` target capacity strategy automatically replenishes the fleet when Spot Instances are interrupted. If an instance is reclaimed, the fleet immediately requests replacement instances from the specified pools. The fleet maintains the target capacity across the configured instance types and AZs, providing automatic fault-tolerant replacement without manual intervention.

distractors.A: A persistent Spot Instance request automatically re-requests a new instance after interruption but for a single instance — it does not manage a fleet or choose optimal pools.
distractors.B: EC2 Auto Scaling with Spot Instances and capacity rebalancing does support automatic replacement and is a valid approach, but Spot Fleet's 'maintain' strategy is the more direct answer for this pattern.
distractors.D: On-Demand capacity reservations guarantee On-Demand capacity in an AZ but they are On-Demand priced — not Spot instances.

question: A Spot Instance receives a 2-minute interruption notice. The application running on it is processing a long-running job that takes 30 minutes. What is the best architectural pattern to handle this gracefully?

options.A: Ignore the interruption notice — the 2 minutes is enough to finish most tasks
options.B: Use instance metadata to detect the interruption notice, checkpoint progress to S3, and terminate gracefully
options.C: Upgrade to a larger instance type to reduce job duration below 2 minutes
options.D: Use a Dedicated Instance to prevent interruptions

explanation: The correct pattern for Spot Instance interruption handling is: (1) Poll the EC2 instance metadata endpoint (`169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/spot/termination-time`) to detect interruption notices. (2) On detection, save the current job's checkpoint/state to a durable store (S3, DynamoDB). (3) Terminate gracefully. When a replacement instance starts, it reads the checkpoint and resumes from where the previous instance stopped. This is the standard approach for long-running workloads on Spot.

distractors.A: 2 minutes is not enough for a 30-minute job — the instance will be terminated and all un-checkpointed progress is lost.
distractors.C: Upgrading instance type does not prevent Spot interruptions — all Spot instances are subject to interruption at AWS's discretion; the job duration is irrelevant.
distractors.D: Dedicated Instances are On-Demand priced instances that run on hardware dedicated to your account — they are not immune to operational interruptions and cost significantly more.

question: A company wants to run Spot Instances for a stateless web tier behind an ALB. They want to maximize Spot availability and minimize the chance of simultaneous interruption across all instances. Which Spot allocation strategy should they use?

options.A: lowest-price — always use the cheapest available Spot pool
options.B: capacity-optimized — launch instances from the pool with the most available capacity
options.C: price-capacity-optimized — balance between lowest price and highest capacity
options.D: diversified — spread instances across all configured pools

explanation: The `price-capacity-optimized` strategy (recommended by AWS since 2022) balances Spot Instance interruption probability with price. It launches from pools with high available capacity (reducing interruption probability) while still optimizing for price. For a web tier where availability matters, this strategy outperforms `lowest-price` (which picks cheap pools that may have fewer instances and higher interruption rates) while being better than `capacity-optimized` alone.

distractors.A: The `lowest-price` strategy selects the cheapest Spot pools, which often have less available capacity and higher interruption rates — the cheapest pool may lose all your instances simultaneously.
distractors.B: The `capacity-optimized` strategy focuses solely on pools with most available capacity, which minimizes interruption but ignores price entirely — `price-capacity-optimized` is now recommended over this.
distractors.D: The `diversified` strategy is a Spot Fleet strategy that spreads instances across pools but doesn't optimize for either price or capacity availability specifically.

question: A data science team uses EC2 Spot Instances for ML training jobs that run for 4-8 hours. They need to be able to pause and resume jobs and want the instances to be automatically hibernated (saving memory state to EBS) when interrupted rather than terminated. Which Spot Instance configuration enables this?

options.A: Configure the Spot request with interruption behavior 'stop' on instances with instance store
options.B: Configure the Spot request with interruption behavior 'hibernate' on EBS-backed instances with enough EBS space
options.C: Use EC2 Hibernate on On-Demand Instances with Spot pricing
options.D: Enable EC2 auto-recovery on Spot Instances

explanation: Spot Instance hibernation saves the instance's in-memory state (RAM contents) to the EBS root volume when interrupted, then restores the state when capacity becomes available again. Requirements: (1) interruption behavior set to 'hibernate', (2) EBS-backed instance (no instance store), (3) EBS root volume has sufficient free space for RAM contents, (4) instance must be configured to support hibernation at launch, (5) RAM ≤ 150 GB. The training job resumes from where it left off.

distractors.A: Instances with instance store cannot hibernate — RAM contents cannot be saved to ephemeral storage since it disappears on interruption. Stop behavior saves instance state in EBS but restores only when you manually start it, not automatically when Spot capacity returns.
distractors.C: EC2 Hibernate is a feature for On-Demand instances to hibernate to EBS — it is separate from Spot hibernation behavior and doesn't provide automatic Spot-capacity-driven resume.
distractors.D: EC2 auto-recovery restores instances after hardware failures (for On-Demand) — it does not apply to Spot Instances or provide hibernation behavior.

question: A company stores compliance audit logs in S3. Logs are accessed frequently for the first 30 days after creation, then rarely accessed for the next 90 days, and must be retained for 7 years for regulatory requirements. Which S3 storage class is most cost-effective for the rarely accessed period (days 31-120)?

options.A: S3 Standard
options.B: S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
options.C: S3 One Zone-IA
options.D: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval

explanation: S3 Standard-IA is designed for data accessed infrequently but requiring rapid access when needed. It costs significantly less per GB stored than S3 Standard (~60% less storage cost) but charges a per-GB retrieval fee. For compliance logs accessed rarely but requiring fast access for audits, S3 Standard-IA provides the right balance. It also maintains multi-AZ durability unlike S3 One Zone-IA.

distractors.A: S3 Standard charges a higher per-GB storage price with no retrieval fee — inefficient for rarely accessed data.
distractors.C: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, reducing durability. Compliance logs should not be stored in a single AZ — if that AZ has an outage, the data is unavailable.
distractors.D: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is for data accessed a few times per year at millisecond retrieval speed — it is cheaper than Standard-IA for storage but has higher retrieval fees. For 'rarely accessed' over 90 days, Glacier might be worth considering but Standard-IA is more practical if retrieval needs are unclear.

question: A company archives large video files that are accessed once or twice per year. When accessed, they can tolerate a retrieval time of up to 5 hours. Which S3 storage class minimizes storage costs?

options.A: S3 Standard-IA
options.B: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
options.C: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
options.D: S3 Glacier Deep Archive

explanation: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 storage class at approximately $0.00099/GB/month — about 23x cheaper than S3 Standard. It is designed for data that is rarely accessed and can tolerate retrieval times of 12 hours (standard) or 48 hours (bulk). For data accessed once or twice per year with a 5-hour tolerance, Glacier Flexible Retrieval (3-5 hours retrieval) or Deep Archive both work, but Deep Archive has lower storage cost. Since 5 hours > Deep Archive's 12-hour standard retrieval, Flexible Retrieval is actually more appropriate if 5 hours is a hard limit.

distractors.A: S3 Standard-IA costs ~$0.0125/GB/month — significantly more than Glacier options for rarely accessed archival data.
distractors.B: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval provides millisecond retrieval at a storage cost similar to Standard-IA — unnecessarily fast and more expensive for data that tolerates hours of retrieval time.
distractors.C: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (3-5 hours standard retrieval) meets the 5-hour requirement and is cheaper than Standard-IA, but Deep Archive is cheaper for storage — though Deep Archive's 12-hour minimum retrieval time exceeds the 5-hour requirement if that is a hard deadline.

question: A company stores thousands of machine learning training datasets in S3. Access patterns are unpredictable — some datasets are accessed daily while others may not be accessed for months. They want to minimize costs without manually managing storage class transitions. Which S3 storage class handles this automatically?

options.A: S3 Standard with lifecycle rules transitioning to Standard-IA after 30 days
options.B: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
options.C: S3 Standard with manual review quarterly
options.D: S3 One Zone-IA for all data

explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically monitors access patterns and moves objects between tiers (Frequent Access, Infrequent Access, Archive Instant Access) without retrieval fees or performance impact. For unpredictable access patterns, it eliminates the risk of paying retrieval fees for unexpectedly accessed Standard-IA data and avoids manual lifecycle policy management. There is a small monthly monitoring fee per object.

distractors.A: Lifecycle rules transitioning to Standard-IA after 30 days are appropriate only when access patterns are predictable. For unpredictable patterns, this forces retrieval fees when datasets are accessed after the 30-day transition.
distractors.C: Manual quarterly review is operationally intensive and reactive — by the time data is reviewed, costs have already been incurred.
distractors.D: S3 One Zone-IA reduces durability (single AZ) and still charges retrieval fees — not appropriate for ML training datasets that may be accessed frequently.

question: A company stores 500 TB of data in S3 Standard. A cost analysis shows that 80% of the data has not been accessed in 6 months. The company wants to minimize storage costs while maintaining the ability to access any file within 1 millisecond if needed. Which storage class transition should they implement?

options.A: Transition to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 180 days
options.B: Transition to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 180 days
options.C: Transition to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, then to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 90 more days
options.D: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering with Archive Instant Access tier

explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering with the Archive Instant Access tier automatically moves objects to Glacier Instant Retrieval (millisecond access, lowest storage cost in Intelligent-Tiering) when not accessed for 90 days, and back to Frequent Access tier when accessed. Since the requirement is millisecond access (not minutes or hours), Glacier Instant Retrieval is the lowest-cost option meeting this SLA. Intelligent-Tiering manages this automatically without lifecycle rules.

distractors.A: Glacier Flexible Retrieval provides 3-5 hour retrieval — this violates the 1-millisecond access requirement.
distractors.B: Glacier Instant Retrieval with a static lifecycle rule would work for the 1ms requirement, but Intelligent-Tiering is better because the 20% of frequently accessed data won't be transitioned and won't incur retrieval fees.
distractors.C: This is a valid manual lifecycle approach but is more complex to manage than Intelligent-Tiering and risks retrieval fees for data that returns to frequent access patterns.

question: A company generates daily log files stored in S3. Logs older than 90 days are rarely accessed and can tolerate a 12-hour retrieval delay. After 1 year, logs must be deleted. Which S3 lifecycle configuration achieves this with minimum cost?

options.A: Transition to Glacier Deep Archive at 90 days; expire at 365 days
options.B: Transition to Standard-IA at 30 days, then expire at 90 days
options.C: Keep in Standard; expire at 365 days
options.D: Transition to Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90 days; transition to Deep Archive at 180 days; expire at 365 days

explanation: Transitioning to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days (the cheapest storage class at ~$0.001/GB/month) satisfies the requirement that logs older than 90 days can tolerate 12-hour retrieval. Setting an expiration of 365 days automatically deletes objects, avoiding indefinite storage costs. This is the simplest, cheapest two-rule lifecycle configuration for this use case.

distractors.B: Expiring at 90 days violates the 1-year retention requirement.
distractors.C: Keeping logs in S3 Standard for the full year costs approximately 100x more than Glacier Deep Archive for rarely accessed data.
distractors.D: Adding an intermediate Glacier Flexible Retrieval tier adds a lifecycle transition fee and doesn't reduce overall cost compared to going directly to Deep Archive at 90 days.

question: A company uses S3 versioning on a bucket. Over time, old versions of objects accumulate. The company wants to automatically delete non-current versions older than 30 days to control storage costs. Which lifecycle rule configuration achieves this?

options.A: Add an expiration rule with a 30-day prefix filter
options.B: Add a NoncurrentVersionExpiration rule with 30 days
options.C: Disable versioning and manually delete old versions
options.D: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering which automatically removes old versions

explanation: The `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` lifecycle action specifically targets non-current (older) versions of versioned objects. Setting it to 30 days automatically permanently deletes non-current versions that are older than 30 days, reclaiming storage. The current version is unaffected. This is the purpose-built lifecycle action for managing versioned object costs.

distractors.A: An expiration rule with a prefix filter deletes the current version of objects, not old non-current versions — this would delete live data.
distractors.C: Disabling versioning stops new versions from being created but does not delete existing non-current versions — and loses the benefits of version history going forward.
distractors.D: Intelligent-Tiering manages storage class transitions for cost optimization but does not delete objects or manage version expiration.

question: A company uses S3 multipart uploads for large video files. Incomplete multipart uploads accumulate over time due to failed uploads, incurring storage charges. Which lifecycle rule stops this?

options.A: NoncurrentVersionExpiration after 1 day
options.B: AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload after a specified number of days
options.C: Transition to Glacier after 0 days
options.D: Enable S3 Object Lock to block incomplete uploads

explanation: The `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle action automatically aborts multipart upload sessions that have not been completed within the specified number of days after initiation. AWS then deletes the associated parts, freeing storage. This is the specific lifecycle action for cleaning up incomplete multipart uploads — a commonly overlooked source of S3 cost.

distractors.A: NoncurrentVersionExpiration removes old non-current versions of versioned objects — it has no effect on incomplete multipart upload parts, which are not stored as versioned objects.
distractors.C: Lifecycle transitions apply to complete objects — they cannot transition incomplete multipart upload parts.
distractors.D: S3 Object Lock prevents deletion of objects for compliance purposes — it does not affect multipart upload sessions and would make it harder to clean up.

question: A company runs a database on EC2 with an EBS volume. The database requires consistent, low-latency I/O performance. The workload needs 3,000 IOPS. Which EBS volume type is the most cost-effective choice?

options.A: io2 Block Express
options.B: gp3 (General Purpose SSD)
options.C: st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD)
options.D: sc1 (Cold HDD)

explanation: gp3 volumes provide a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s throughput at no extra cost, with the ability to provision up to 16,000 IOPS independently of storage size. For a 3,000 IOPS requirement, gp3 at the baseline covers the need at ~$0.08/GB/month — significantly cheaper than io2 Block Express which charges per-IOPS additionally. gp3 is now the recommended default EBS volume type.

distractors.A: io2 Block Express provides up to 256,000 IOPS and is designed for mission-critical I/O-intensive databases (Oracle, SAP HANA) at a much higher cost — overkill for 3,000 IOPS.
distractors.C: st1 is a throughput-optimized HDD for sequential large-block workloads (big data, log processing) — it provides low IOPS and high latency, unsuitable for databases requiring consistent low-latency I/O.
distractors.D: sc1 is the lowest-cost HDD for infrequently accessed, sequential cold data — very low IOPS and highest latency, completely unsuitable for database workloads.

question: A company has 200 EC2 instances each with a gp2 EBS volume sized at 500 GB (which provides 1,500 IOPS on gp2). Analysis shows actual IOPS usage averages only 500 IOPS. They are considering migrating to gp3. What is the cost benefit of switching to gp3?

options.A: gp3 is the same price as gp2 with identical IOPS — no benefit
options.B: gp3 costs 20% less per GB than gp2 and provides 3,000 IOPS baseline regardless of size, reducing over-provisioning
options.C: gp3 is more expensive than gp2 but provides better performance — trade cost for performance
options.D: gp2 cannot be converted to gp3 — new volumes must be created

explanation: gp3 costs ~$0.08/GB/month versus gp2's ~$0.10/GB/month — a 20% storage cost reduction. Additionally, gp3 provides a fixed 3,000 IOPS baseline regardless of volume size, while gp2 provides 3 IOPS/GB (so 500 GB gp2 gives only 1,500 IOPS). Companies that over-provisioned gp2 volume size to get more IOPS can right-size to smaller gp3 volumes. Existing gp2 volumes can be modified in-place to gp3 with zero downtime.

distractors.A: gp3 costs 20% less than gp2 per GB and provides 2x the baseline IOPS for the same size volume.
distractors.C: gp3 is cheaper and provides better baseline performance than gp2 — it is strictly better for most workloads.
distractors.D: Existing EBS volumes can be modified from gp2 to gp3 in-place using the Elastic Volumes feature with no downtime required.

question: A company has EBS snapshots accumulating in S3 from daily automated backups of a 2 TB volume over 3 years. The snapshots occupy 50 TB of S3 storage. How does EBS snapshot storage actually work, and what is the most cost-effective way to manage this?

options.A: Each snapshot stores the full 2 TB — delete old snapshots to free exactly 2 TB per deleted snapshot
options.B: Snapshots are incremental — each stores only changed blocks since the previous snapshot; use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager to automate retention policies
options.C: Snapshots are stored in Standard S3 and accrue standard S3 charges — move them to Glacier manually to reduce cost
options.D: Only the first snapshot is stored fully — subsequent snapshots are zero-cost pointers

explanation: EBS snapshots are incremental — the first snapshot stores all blocks, and subsequent snapshots store only blocks that changed since the last snapshot. When you delete a snapshot, only the unique blocks that no other snapshot references are deleted; referenced blocks are preserved. Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) to create automated snapshot schedules with retention policies (e.g., keep 7 daily, 4 weekly, 12 monthly) to automatically delete old snapshots while maintaining the needed recovery points.

distractors.A: Deleting a snapshot does not free the full 2 TB — only unique unreferenced blocks are deleted. The amount freed depends on how many blocks changed since adjacent snapshots.
distractors.C: EBS snapshots are stored in a managed S3 infrastructure owned by AWS — you cannot access them as S3 objects or move them to Glacier. They are charged at the EBS snapshot rate, not standard S3 rates.
distractors.D: Only the first snapshot stores all blocks; subsequent snapshots are incremental (not zero-cost) — they store the changed blocks.

question: A company processes image thumbnails triggered by S3 uploads. The function runs for 500ms and is invoked 1 million times per month. Which pricing model applies to AWS Lambda?

options.A: Per-hour billing based on the number of Lambda functions deployed
options.B: Per-request + per-GB-second of compute (duration × memory), with a free tier
options.C: Reserved capacity billing regardless of invocations
options.D: Per-GB of code storage plus per-request

explanation: Lambda pricing has two components: (1) requests: $0.20 per 1 million requests (first 1 million free per month), and (2) duration: charged per GB-second (memory allocation × duration in seconds) at $0.0000166667 per GB-second. The free tier provides 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds per month. This pay-per-use model means you pay only when code runs, making Lambda very cost-effective for intermittent workloads.

distractors.A: Lambda does not charge per deployed function — there is no cost for having a function deployed that receives no invocations.
distractors.C: Reserved capacity billing applies to Reserved Instances and Savings Plans for EC2, not Lambda. Lambda charges are purely usage-based unless Provisioned Concurrency is configured.
distractors.D: Lambda does not charge for code storage beyond 75 GB total (which is part of the free tier) — billing is dominated by requests and duration.

question: A Lambda function is currently configured with 512 MB of memory and runs for 10 seconds. A developer increases memory to 1024 MB and the function now runs for 4 seconds. What is the effect on Lambda cost?

options.A: Cost doubles because memory doubled
options.B: Cost decreases by 20% — reduced duration more than offsets the higher memory
options.C: Cost is the same — the GB-seconds consumed are equal
options.D: Cost increases by 60% — more memory always costs more

explanation: Lambda cost = memory (GB) × duration (seconds). Original: 0.5 GB × 10s = 5 GB-seconds. New: 1 GB × 4s = 4 GB-seconds. The new configuration uses 4/5 = 80% of the original GB-seconds, a 20% cost reduction. Allocating more memory to Lambda functions often improves performance enough that reduced duration more than compensates for the higher memory cost. AWS Lambda Power Tuning tool helps find the optimal memory setting.

distractors.A: Doubling memory does not double cost if duration decreases proportionally — cost depends on GB-seconds (memory × time).
distractors.C: 5 GB-seconds (original) ≠ 4 GB-seconds (new) — the GB-seconds decreased by 20%.
distractors.D: Cost decreased, not increased — the faster execution with more memory uses fewer total GB-seconds.

question: A company uses API Gateway REST API with Lambda integration and processes 100 million API calls per month. They are considering switching to HTTP API. What is the primary cost difference?

options.A: HTTP API costs about 71% less per million API calls than REST API
options.B: HTTP API and REST API have identical pricing
options.C: REST API is cheaper because it includes caching at no extra cost
options.D: HTTP API charges per connection, while REST API charges per request

explanation: API Gateway HTTP API costs $1.00 per million requests (after free tier), while REST API costs $3.50 per million requests — HTTP API is approximately 71% cheaper. HTTP API is purpose-built for modern Lambda and HTTP backends with lower latency as well. The trade-off is HTTP API lacks some REST API features (usage plans, caching, mapping templates), but for simple Lambda integrations, HTTP API provides significant cost savings.

distractors.B: HTTP API is significantly cheaper than REST API — they have different pricing models.
distractors.C: API Gateway caching for REST API is an additional cost (charged per cache size-hour) — it is not included at no extra cost.
distractors.D: API Gateway (both REST and HTTP) charges per request, not per connection. WebSocket API charges per connection-minute.

question: A company has a VPC with private subnets in 3 AZs. All private EC2 instances route internet-bound traffic through a single NAT Gateway in one AZ. What is the primary cost concern with this architecture?

options.A: The NAT Gateway will become a single point of failure and will increase EC2 costs
options.B: Cross-AZ data transfer charges apply when instances in other AZs send traffic through the NAT Gateway in a different AZ
options.C: The NAT Gateway has no data processing charges — only hourly charges apply
options.D: Private instances cannot use NAT Gateways for internet access — NAT instances must be used instead

explanation: AWS charges for cross-AZ data transfer at $0.01/GB in each direction. When an EC2 instance in us-east-1b sends traffic through a NAT Gateway in us-east-1a, there is a $0.01/GB charge from the instance to the NAT Gateway, PLUS the NAT Gateway data processing charge ($0.045/GB), PLUS potentially egress charges. For high-throughput workloads, placing a NAT Gateway in each AZ where private instances exist eliminates cross-AZ charges at the cost of additional hourly NAT Gateway fees.

distractors.A: A single NAT Gateway is indeed a single point of failure (an AZ failure affects all instances), but the question asks about cost concerns, not availability.
distractors.C: NAT Gateway charges BOTH hourly ($0.045/hour) AND per-GB data processing ($0.045/GB) — both are significant costs.
distractors.D: NAT Gateways are the AWS-managed recommended solution for private subnet internet access — NAT instances are the older, self-managed alternative.

question: A company's EC2 instances in private subnets frequently access Amazon S3 in the same region. Currently, this traffic goes through a NAT Gateway. What architectural change eliminates NAT Gateway data processing charges for S3 traffic while also improving security?

options.A: Move the EC2 instances to public subnets with direct internet access
options.B: Create an S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint in the VPC and update route tables
options.C: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration instead of standard S3 access
options.D: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in a public subnet

explanation: An S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint routes S3 traffic through the AWS private network directly from the VPC to S3, bypassing the NAT Gateway entirely. Gateway endpoints for S3 (and DynamoDB) are free — there is no hourly cost or data processing charge. Traffic never leaves the AWS network, improving security. You simply add the endpoint to the VPC and update route tables in the private subnets to route S3 prefixes through the endpoint.

distractors.A: Moving instances to public subnets exposes them directly to the internet, violating the security principle of keeping backend instances private.
distractors.C: S3 Transfer Acceleration is designed for accelerating cross-region or internet uploads to S3 using CloudFront edge locations — it costs more than standard S3 access and does not eliminate NAT Gateway charges.
distractors.D: Cross-Region Replication copies objects to another region — it does not affect how private subnet instances access S3 and would incur replication costs.

question: Which of the following data transfer scenarios in AWS incurs NO data transfer charges?

options.A: EC2 instance in us-east-1 transferring data to an S3 bucket in eu-west-1
options.B: CloudFront distributing data to end users from its edge caches
options.C: Data transferred INTO AWS from the internet (ingress)
options.D: EC2 instance in us-east-1a sending data to an EC2 instance in us-east-1b

explanation: AWS does not charge for data transferred INTO AWS from the internet (inbound/ingress). This includes uploading files to S3, sending data to EC2 instances, etc. AWS charges for data transferred OUT of AWS to the internet (egress), between regions, and in some cases between AZs. This pricing structure encourages keeping data in AWS.

distractors.A: Cross-region data transfer is charged — transferring from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 incurs both the S3 PUT request cost and cross-region transfer fees.
distractors.B: CloudFront charges for data transferred to end users (egress from CloudFront), though at lower rates than direct EC2 egress.
distractors.D: Data transfer between AZs within the same region is charged at $0.01/GB in each direction (except for certain services like S3 and some managed services).

question: A company serves 100 TB of video content per month to users worldwide directly from EC2 instances. They want to reduce egress costs. Which solution most reduces data transfer costs?

options.A: Use S3 instead of EC2 to serve content
options.B: Use Amazon CloudFront as a CDN in front of the S3 or EC2 origin
options.C: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
options.D: Use AWS Direct Connect for all user connections

explanation: CloudFront charges significantly less for data transfer out to users than direct EC2 or S3 egress — CloudFront prices start at $0.085/GB versus EC2's $0.09/GB for the first 10 TB, with CloudFront scaling to much lower prices at volume ($0.02/GB at 5 PB+). Additionally, repeated requests for the same content are served from cache, reducing origin traffic. For 100 TB/month, CloudFront provides both cost reduction and better global performance.

distractors.A: S3 charges similar egress rates to EC2 for internet transfer — moving from EC2 to S3 alone doesn't significantly reduce data transfer costs.
distractors.C: S3 Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations but is designed for accelerating uploads INTO S3, not for serving content to users. It costs more than standard S3 egress.
distractors.D: Direct Connect is for connecting corporate data centers to AWS — end users cannot use Direct Connect for video streaming.

question: A company wants a quick assessment of their AWS environment for cost savings opportunities, security gaps, and service limit checks without building custom tooling. Which AWS service provides these checks automatically?

options.A: AWS Config
options.B: Amazon Inspector
options.C: AWS Trusted Advisor
options.D: AWS Security Hub

explanation: AWS Trusted Advisor provides automated best-practice checks across five categories: Cost Optimization (e.g., idle EC2 instances, underutilized RIs), Security (e.g., exposed S3 buckets, unrestricted security groups), Fault Tolerance (e.g., missing Multi-AZ), Performance (e.g., overutilized EC2), and Service Limits. Basic checks are available to all customers; Business and Enterprise Support plans unlock all checks with real-time monitoring.

distractors.A: AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes and evaluates compliance against rules — it does not provide cost optimization recommendations or limit checks.
distractors.B: Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability assessment service for EC2 instances and container images — it focuses on security vulnerabilities, not cost or limits.
distractors.D: AWS Security Hub aggregates security findings from multiple services — it focuses on security posture, not cost optimization or service limits.

question: AWS Trusted Advisor flags 15 EC2 instances as 'underutilized' with CPU utilization below 10% for 14 days. The instances are reserved with 1-year Standard RIs. What is the most cost-effective response?

options.A: Terminate all 15 instances immediately to stop EC2 charges
options.B: Downsize the instances to a smaller instance type that fits actual utilization, and modify the RIs to match
options.C: Purchase additional RIs to cover the underutilized instances
options.D: Enable auto-scaling to scale down to zero during low-utilization periods

explanation: Trusted Advisor identifies underutilized instances, but terminating them while their RIs remain active wastes the RI commitment (you still pay). The optimal response is to downsize instances to a smaller type that matches actual usage (e.g., m5.2xlarge to m5.large), then modify the Standard RIs using normalization factor matching (larger RIs can cover multiple smaller instances of the same family). This reduces running costs while maximizing RI value.

distractors.A: Terminating instances without addressing the RI commitment means you continue paying for the RI (which applies to any on-demand instance of that family/size) — the cost savings come from right-sizing, not just termination.
distractors.C: Purchasing more RIs for underutilized instances further over-commits capacity — the issue is over-provisioning, not under-reservation.
distractors.D: Auto-scaling to zero means the service is unavailable during scale-down periods — this may not be acceptable for production workloads, and RIs still charge during idle periods.

question: A company wants to receive an alert when their AWS monthly spend is projected to exceed $10,000 before the end of the month. Which AWS service enables this?

options.A: AWS Cost Explorer with saved reports
options.B: AWS Budgets with a cost budget and alert threshold
options.C: AWS Trusted Advisor service limit checks
options.D: Amazon CloudWatch billing alarm

explanation: AWS Budgets allows you to set custom cost, usage, and reservation budgets with alert thresholds. A cost budget can alert you when actual spend reaches a percentage threshold OR when forecasted spend is projected to exceed the budget. Alerts are sent via email or SNS. This is the purpose-built service for proactive cost alerting.

distractors.A: Cost Explorer is for analyzing historical and current costs and forecasting — it does not send proactive alerts when spend approaches a threshold.
distractors.C: Trusted Advisor service limit checks alert on approaching service limits, not on billing amounts.
distractors.D: CloudWatch billing alarms do exist and can alert on estimated charges, but AWS Budgets provides more sophisticated forecasted spend alerts and is the recommended modern solution.

question: A FinOps team wants to analyze which specific EC2 instance types and services are driving the most cost increase over the past 3 months, broken down by team (using cost allocation tags). Which AWS service provides this analysis?

options.A: AWS Trusted Advisor
options.B: AWS Cost Explorer
options.C: AWS Budgets
options.D: AWS Pricing Calculator

explanation: AWS Cost Explorer provides interactive visualizations of AWS cost and usage data with filtering and grouping by service, linked account, tag, region, instance type, and more. The team can use cost allocation tags (e.g., `team:engineering`) to break down costs by team and identify which instance types are driving cost increases. Cost Explorer also provides rightsizing recommendations and RI/Savings Plan coverage reports.

distractors.A: Trusted Advisor provides high-level checks and recommendations but does not offer detailed historical cost analysis by tag or instance type.
distractors.C: AWS Budgets tracks spend against defined budgets and sends alerts — it does not provide the interactive analytical queries and groupings that Cost Explorer offers.
distractors.D: AWS Pricing Calculator estimates costs for planned architectures before deployment — it does not analyze actual historical spend.

question: A company has 50 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations. They want to enforce a spending limit where each account cannot exceed $5,000/month, and if any account is projected to exceed $4,500, the DevOps team is automatically notified and the account's IAM permissions are restricted. Which combination of services implements this?

options.A: AWS Budgets + AWS Budgets Actions + SNS notifications
options.B: AWS Cost Explorer + CloudWatch alarms + SCPs
options.C: AWS Trusted Advisor + AWS Config remediation
options.D: AWS Pricing Calculator + AWS Organizations SCPs

explanation: AWS Budgets Actions allows you to define automated actions triggered when a budget threshold is breached: (1) Apply an IAM policy or SCP to restrict permissions, (2) Stop EC2/RDS instances, or (3) Send an SNS notification. By creating a budget for each account at $4,500 (90% of $5,000 limit), you can automatically restrict IAM permissions and notify the DevOps team when spend approaches the limit — no manual intervention required.

distractors.B: Cost Explorer + CloudWatch alarms can trigger notifications but cannot automatically apply IAM policy restrictions — Budgets Actions is the purpose-built automated remediation solution.
distractors.C: Trusted Advisor + Config remediation addresses configuration compliance, not billing-based automated permission restriction.
distractors.D: AWS Pricing Calculator is for estimating costs before deployment — it cannot monitor actual spend or trigger automated actions.

question: A solutions architect wants to identify EC2 instances that are over-provisioned (paying for more compute than needed) across a large AWS account with 500+ instances. The recommendation should be based on actual CloudWatch metrics. Which service provides machine-learning-based rightsizing recommendations?

options.A: AWS Trusted Advisor underutilized instance checks
options.B: AWS Compute Optimizer
options.C: AWS Cost Explorer rightsizing recommendations
options.D: AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager

explanation: AWS Compute Optimizer uses machine learning to analyze CloudWatch utilization metrics (CPU, memory with CloudWatch agent, network, disk I/O) and recommends optimal AWS resource configurations. For EC2, it recommends the right instance type and size based on actual workload patterns. It considers IOPS, memory, and network alongside CPU — providing more nuanced recommendations than simple CPU-threshold checks.

distractors.A: Trusted Advisor's underutilized check uses a simple 14-day average CPU threshold (<10%) — it is less sophisticated than Compute Optimizer's ML-based multi-dimensional analysis.
distractors.C: Cost Explorer rightsizing recommendations also suggest instance downsizing but are based primarily on CPU utilization — Compute Optimizer provides deeper multi-metric analysis including memory.
distractors.D: AWS Systems Manager Fleet Manager provides visibility into EC2 fleet inventory and operations but does not provide rightsizing or cost optimization recommendations.

question: AWS Compute Optimizer recommends downsizing an m5.4xlarge EC2 instance to an m5.xlarge (75% smaller). A solutions architect is concerned the recommendation might be wrong because the instance handles occasional large batch jobs. What should the architect verify before acting on the recommendation?

options.A: The Compute Optimizer recommendation is always correct — implement immediately
options.B: Check the p99 CPU and memory utilization metrics, not just averages, to ensure the smaller instance handles peak load
options.C: Increase the observation period in Compute Optimizer from 14 to 30 days
options.D: Purchase a Reserved Instance for the m5.xlarge before downsizing

explanation: Compute Optimizer recommendations are based on CPU and memory utilization statistics including p99 (99th percentile). However, architects should review the p99 data in the Compute Optimizer console to ensure peaks during batch jobs are captured. If batch jobs spike CPU to 90%+ occasionally, the m5.xlarge may not have sufficient headroom. Verifying peak utilization patterns before downsizing prevents performance degradation.

distractors.A: Compute Optimizer recommendations are data-driven but should be validated against business requirements (peak loads, latency SLAs) before implementation.
distractors.C: Compute Optimizer uses up to 14 days of CloudWatch metrics — this is configurable but the architect should first validate existing recommendations against peak utilization before extending the observation period.
distractors.D: Purchasing an RI before validating the recommendation is premature — right-size first, then commit to RIs or Savings Plans for the right-sized instances.

question: A company wants to allocate AWS costs to individual business units (Engineering, Marketing, Sales). Each business unit has its own AWS resources. Which AWS feature enables cost tracking and reporting by business unit?

options.A: AWS Organizations Service Control Policies
options.B: Cost Allocation Tags with AWS Cost Explorer
options.C: AWS Budgets with per-account limits
options.D: AWS Config compliance rules

explanation: Cost Allocation Tags allow you to label AWS resources with metadata (e.g., `department:engineering`) that appears in cost reports. After activating tags as cost allocation tags in the Billing console, AWS Cost Explorer can group and filter costs by tag. This enables chargebacks and showback reporting to individual business units based on their tagged resource consumption.

distractors.A: SCPs restrict what actions accounts or OUs can take — they enforce permissions but do not track or allocate costs.
distractors.C: AWS Budgets can create per-account spending alerts but accounts must map 1:1 to business units — cost allocation tags are more flexible and work within a single account.
distractors.D: AWS Config rules evaluate resource configuration compliance — they do not track or allocate costs.

question: A company runs Lambda functions, ECS Fargate tasks, and EC2 Spot Instances for machine learning inference. They want to reduce compute costs across all three service types with a single pricing commitment. Which AWS service and plan type covers all three?

options.A: EC2 Instance Savings Plans covering Lambda, Fargate, and Spot
options.B: Compute Savings Plans covering EC2, Lambda, and Fargate usage
options.C: Reserved Instances for EC2, plus separate Lambda Provisioned Concurrency commitments
options.D: Spot Instance blocks for predictable savings across all compute types

explanation: Compute Savings Plans (CSP) automatically apply to eligible compute usage — EC2 instances (any family, size, AZ, region, OS, tenancy), AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda. A single hourly spend commitment (e.g., $X/hour) provides up to 66% savings vs. On-Demand across all three compute types simultaneously. CSP is the most flexible savings plan type and is the only one that covers Lambda and Fargate.

distractors.A: EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply only to a specific EC2 instance family in a region — they do not cover Lambda or Fargate.
distractors.C: Reserved Instances only apply to EC2 and some other managed services — Lambda Provisioned Concurrency commitments are separate and do not cover Fargate or Spot.
distractors.D: Spot Instance blocks (fixed duration Spot) only apply to EC2 Spot Instances — they do not cover Lambda or Fargate at all.

question: A company's AWS bill increased 40% month-over-month. AWS Cost Explorer shows the increase is from EC2 data transfer costs. The company has EC2 instances in us-east-1 communicating with RDS in us-east-1. Why might cross-AZ data transfer be unexpectedly high, and what is the fix?

options.A: RDS Multi-AZ creates a standby in a different AZ; EC2 instances in other AZs pay cross-AZ transfer to reach the primary — fix by placing EC2 instances in the same AZ as the RDS primary
options.B: EC2 to RDS communication is always charged for cross-region transfer — move RDS to the same region as EC2
options.C: Data transfer between EC2 and RDS is free regardless of AZ — the cost must be from S3 access
options.D: RDS charges egress fees that EC2 does not — switch to Aurora to eliminate these fees

explanation: When EC2 instances in us-east-1b communicate with an RDS instance whose primary is in us-east-1a, AWS charges $0.01/GB in each direction for cross-AZ data transfer. For database-heavy applications with GB/day of queries and results, this adds up significantly. The fix is to place EC2 instances in the same AZ as the RDS primary endpoint, or better yet, use an RDS Proxy that intelligently routes to the correct AZ. Note: this trades AZ-level resilience for cost.

distractors.B: EC2 and RDS within the same region are not subject to cross-region charges — cross-AZ charges within the same region are the issue.
distractors.C: EC2-to-RDS cross-AZ data transfer IS charged at $0.01/GB per direction — it is not free.
distractors.D: Aurora and RDS have similar cross-AZ data transfer costs — the service type does not eliminate cross-AZ charges.
